summary:
Analog Atlas is a web app that searches the whole Earth for places that resemble a chosen landing or base site on the Moon or Mars. You pick a target: Jezero or Gale crater on Mars, or the Shackleton rim or Marius Hills on the Moon. Analog Atlas scores 334,741 land cells (0.25°, about 28 km) on temperature, slope, rain, vegetation, ice, permafrost, dust and rock type, using NASA data from MODIS, MERRA-2, GPM, MOLA, LOLA and LRO Diviner. Each place gets a 0-100 score with a breakdown by variable. It
 also says plainly what Earth cannot reproduce, such as lunar night cold, vacuum and gravity. Filters for volcanic rock, salt flats and carbonates, a layer of known lava tubes, and a discovery mode that hides the 17 famous analog sites help teams find new, less-studied places. This matters because analog sites are usually chosen by habit or access. Analog Atlas makes the choice transparent, comparable and reproducible, so missions can rehearse where Earth really behaves like their target.
details:
What it does

Analog Atlas answers one question: where on Earth should we rehearse a mission to this site on the Moon or Mars?

The user works through four steps:

  1. Search: pick a target site, or describe a goal in plain words.
  2. Compare: see Earth, the Moon and Mars side by side.
  3. Explore: see the best-matching places on a satellite map of the whole planet.
  4. Place: open one place for its score breakdown, a side-by-side image with the target at the same scale (NASA Mars Trek and Moon Trek), a 3D relief view, and a downloadable brief.

How it works

We built a table of 334,741 land cells (0.25°) with Google Earth Engine. Each cell has these values:

  • Day and night surface temperature and their difference (MODIS)
  • Vegetation (NDVI), barren ground, snow and ice (MODIS)
  • Rain (GPM IMERG)
  • Airborne dust (MERRA-2)
  • Elevation and slope (ETOPO1)
  • Rock type: volcanic, sediment, salt flats and carbonate (GLiM)

For each target we took the same variables from NASA PDS products (MOLA, LOLA, LRO Diviner) and from rover measurements (Curiosity REMS, Perseverance MEDA). Every reference value cites its source.

The engine turns each difference into a 0-1 similarity and combines them with a weighted geometric mean, so one big mismatch pulls the score down. Temperatures that Earth can never reach are listed apart instead of hiding every result.

Coverage of the challenge dimensions

  • Geology: rock type, including salt flats and carbonates.
  • Terrain: slope, elevation and 3D relief.
  • Temperature: day, night and the swing between them.
  • Water and ice: ice, snow, frozen ground and rain.
  • Dust: airborne dust.
  • Habitability: no vegetation and dryness.
  • Caves: a layer of known lava tubes (NASA BRAILLE at Lava Beds, ESA PANGAEA in Lanzarote, and others).
  • Mobility: slope and mission-test suggestions.

Benefits and impact

  • Validation: 14 of the 17 well-known analog sites (Atacama, Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys and others) rank in Earth's top 20% for at least one target, which shows the method recovers the places scientists already use.
  • Discovery mode: it hides those famous sites, so teams, students and countries without a famous analog can find less-studied candidates, including in Latin America.
  • Robustness: a sensitivity test shows how stable the Top 10 is when the weights change.

Creativity

  • We rank Earth by "how alike is it", not by "how extreme is it".
  • We are honest about the limits: each place card says where the analogy breaks.
  • The score is explained so anyone can read it. The main number is "Top X% of Earth's land", because a low absolute score can still be one of the best places on the planet.
Factors we considered
  • Data quality: coverage over 95% of land cells per variable.
  • Traceable sources: every value has a citation.
  • Known limits: a 28 km cell hides small craters and single lava tubes. Rain is a median month, so very seasonal climates look drier than their yearly total. Earth has no low gravity or vacuum.
  • Usability: it works on phones, and has dark and light modes.

Tools

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript.
  • Data processing: Google Earth Engine; pandas, numpy, rasterio and pyarrow.
  • Server: FastAPI and Uvicorn.
  • Web app: React 18, Vite and MapLibre GL.
  • Deployment: Docker on a VPS.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped with background research, code and documentation. Details are in USO_DE_IA_Y_FUENTES.md.
